name: Suleiman the Magnificent
info: Suleiman I, known as Suleiman the Magnificent, was the Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, whose long reign of conquest, lawmaking and building is regarded as the peak of the Ottoman Empire's power.

facts.born: Probably 6 November 1494, at Trabzon on the southern coast of the Black Sea; son of Şehzade Selim (later Sultan Selim I) of the Ottoman dynasty and Hafsa Sultan
facts.died: 6 September 1566, in his tent at the siege of Szigetvár in Hungary, one day before the fortress fell; his death was kept secret for 48 days
facts.role: Governor of Kaffa, then of Manisa, from the age of seventeen; tenth Ottoman sultan, 1520–1566
facts.known: The longest reign of any Ottoman sultan; the capture of Belgrade and Rhodes; the victory at Mohács; the failed siege of Vienna; the conquest of Baghdad; a single code of sultanic law; the Süleymaniye complex built by Mimar Sinan; poetry under the name Muhibbi

t: Suleiman reigned for 46 years, the longest of any Ottoman sultan, and raised the number of the empire's subjects to at least 25 million.
His armies took Belgrade, Rhodes, most of Hungary and Iraq, but were turned back at Vienna in 1529 and at Malta in 1565.
He issued a single code of sultanic law that lasted more than three hundred years, and had his eldest surviving son Mustafa and his son Bayezid put to death in the struggle over the succession.
dyk: Suleiman wrote poetry in Persian and Turkish under the pen name Muhibbi, "Lover", and some of his verses have become Turkish proverbs. When his son Mehmed died in 1543 he composed a chronogram whose letters add up to 955, the year in the Islamic calendar.
ev: Suleiman succeeds his father Selim I as the tenth Ottoman sultan
He besieges and takes Belgrade from the Kingdom of Hungary
Rhodes capitulates after a five-month siege, and the Knights Hospitaller are allowed to depart
He defeats Louis II of Hungary at the Battle of Mohács, where the king and much of the Hungarian aristocracy are killed
His siege of Vienna fails, the first defeat inflicted on him
He makes a grand entrance into Baghdad during the war with the Safavids
His eldest surviving son, Şehzade Mustafa, is killed in his father's tent on his orders
He dies in his tent at the siege of Szigetvár and is succeeded by his son Selim II

sections.early:
Suleiman was born at Trabzon, on the southern coast of the Black Sea, probably on 6 November 1494, although the date is not known with certainty. His father was Şehzade Selim, the later Sultan Selim I; his mother, Hafsa Sultan, was a concubine and convert to Islam of unknown origins, who died in 1534. At the age of seven he began to study science, history, literature, theology and military tactics in the schools of the Topkapı Palace in Constantinople.

At seventeen he was appointed governor, first of Kaffa (Theodosia) and then of Manisa, with a brief tenure at Edirne. At Manisa the concubine Mahidevran entered his harem, and his first sons were born there, among them Mustafa in about 1516 or 1517. As a young man he befriended Ibrahim, originally a Christian from Parga in Epirus, who had been captured in a raid during the Ottoman–Venetian War of 1499–1503 and was given to Suleiman as a slave, most likely in 1514. Ibrahim converted to Islam, and Suleiman made him royal falconer and then first officer of the Royal Bedchamber.

The empire he was to inherit had been built by nine sultans before him. His great-grandfather Mehmed II had failed to take Belgrade because of John Hunyadi's defence, and after the defeats of the Albanians, Bosniaks, Bulgarians, Byzantines and Serbs, the Hungarians and Croats remained the only formidable force that could block further Ottoman gains in Europe. His father, Selim I, who reigned from 1512 to 1520 and wrote poetry in Persian, had made war with the Shia Safavids of Persia a high priority.
sections.rise:
On the death of Selim I, Suleiman entered Constantinople and ascended the throne as the tenth Ottoman sultan, on 30 September 1520. A few weeks later the Venetian envoy Bartolomeo Contarini described him as "tall and slender but tough, with a thin and bony face", and reported the rumour that he "enjoys reading, is knowledgeable and shows good judgment". In 1521 the Ottoman-appointed governor of Damascus led a revolt.

Suleiman turned first against the Kingdom of Hungary. He encircled Belgrade on 28 August 1521, with 250,000 soldiers and over 100 ships, and bombarded it from an island in the Danube. The city became the seat of an Ottoman province. The road to Hungary and Austria lay open, but he turned instead to Rhodes, the base of the Knights Hospitaller. After a five-month siege in 1522 the island capitulated, and he allowed the Knights to depart; the conquest cost the Ottomans 50,000 to 60,000 dead from battle and sickness, and Christian claims went higher.

In 1523 he raised Ibrahim Pasha to Grand Vizier and commander-in-chief of all the armies, and made him beylerbey of Rumelia, with authority over all Ottoman territories in Europe. Ibrahim was about thirty and lacked military expertise, and it is said that tongues wagged at a promotion straight from palace service to the two highest offices of the empire. On 29 August 1526 Suleiman defeated Louis II of Hungary at the Battle of Mohács. The king and much of the Hungarian aristocracy were killed, the royal army was destroyed, and the Jagiellonian dynasty ended in Hungary and Bohemia.
sections.deeds:
After Mohács Hungary was partitioned between the Ottoman Empire, the Habsburg monarchy and the Principality of Transylvania. In the east Suleiman fought three campaigns against the Safavid shah Tahmasp. He made a grand entrance into Baghdad in 1535, and the Peace of Amasya of 1555 gave the Ottomans most of Iraq, with access to the Persian Gulf, and divided Armenia and Georgia between the two empires. At sea he appointed Khair ad Din, known to Europeans as Barbarossa, admiral-in-chief and charged him with rebuilding the fleet. Aden was captured in 1538 and Tripoli in 1551, and he accepted an alliance with Francis I of France against Charles V, which was renewed in 1542.

In Turkish he is known as Kanuni, "the Lawgiver". The Sharia was outside the sultan's power to change, but the Kanuns, covering criminal law, land tenure and taxation, depended on his will alone. He collected the judgments of the nine sultans before him, removed duplications and contradictions, and, supported by his Grand Mufti Ebussuud, issued a single code that was to last more than three hundred years. New criminal legislation prescribed fines for specific offences and reduced the instances requiring death or mutilation. In late 1553 or 1554 he issued a firman denouncing blood libels against the Jews.

Under his patronage, imperial societies of craftsmen worked at the Topkapı Palace; a register of 1526 lists 40 societies with over 600 members. Mimar Sinan, chief court architect from 1538, built for him the Süleymaniye complex in Constantinople between 1550 and 1557.
sections.opponents:
His principal enemies were the Habsburgs Charles V and Ferdinand I, the Safavid shah, the Portuguese and the Knights of St. John. At Vienna in the autumn of 1529 a reinforced garrison of 16,000 men inflicted the first defeat on him; a second attempt in 1532 was delayed by the siege of Güns and never reached the city. In both cases bad weather forced the army to leave siege equipment behind, and supply lines were overstretched. Shah Tahmasp avoided pitched battle, gave up territory and used scorched earth tactics, so that the campaign of 1548–1549 was abandoned and that of 1553 ended in stalemate. In 1535 Charles V led a Holy League of 26,700 soldiers to victory over the Ottomans at Tunis, and an Ottoman fleet failed against the Portuguese at Diu in 1538.

There was opposition within the empire as well. While he campaigned in Hungary in 1526, Turkmen tribes in Cilicia revolted under Kalender Çelebi. At court the rapid rise and vast wealth of Ibrahim Pasha made the Grand Vizier many enemies; Ibrahim had the finance secretary İskender Çelebi sentenced to death, and by supporting Mustafa as heir he came into dispute with Hürrem Sultan. After thirteen years in office he fell from favour, and Suleiman had him strangled in his sleep.

Hürrem, a former slave from Ruthenia, became the sultan's legal wife in 1534, to the astonishment of observers, and the powers he granted her gave rise to rumours at court that he had been bewitched. Modern historians caution that assessments of the reign have often credited to Suleiman alone what was the work of many who served him.
sections.last:
The last decades of the reign were marked by the struggle over the succession. Until the reign of Ahmed I the empire had no formal means of naming a successor, and successions usually involved the death of competing princes. Four of his sons lived into the 1550s: Mustafa, the eldest, born to Mahidevran, and Selim, Bayezid and Cihangir, born to Hürrem. Hürrem is usually held at least partly responsible for the intrigues, though there is no evidence to support this. During the Persian campaign the Grand Vizier Rüstem spread rumours that Mustafa was receptive to the idea of replacing his father. Suleiman summoned Mustafa to his tent in the Ereğli valley, where he was killed with a bow-string; the execution is dated 6 October 1553.

Civil war then broke out between Selim and Bayezid. With the aid of his father's army Selim defeated Bayezid at Konya in 1559, and Bayezid fled to the Safavids with his four sons. In return for large amounts of gold the Shah allowed a Turkish executioner to strangle Bayezid and his sons in 1561. In 1565 the Ottomans besieged Malta from 18 May to 8 September; a relief force from Spain turned the battle, with the loss of 10,000 Ottoman troops.

On 1 May 1566, after an absence of some thirteen years, Suleiman set out on his thirteenth expedition, against Szigetvár in Hungary. He died in his tent on 6 September, one day before the fortress fell. The Grand Vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha kept the death secret for 48 days, until Selim II could be enthroned. The body was taken to Istanbul and buried in a mausoleum at the Süleymaniye Mosque.
sections.legacy:
Suleiman's conquests brought major Muslim cities, many Balkan provinces and most of North Africa under Ottoman control, and gave the empire a powerful presence in the European balance of power. Austria's ambassador Busbecq warned that once the Turks had settled with Persia, "they will fly at our throats supported by the might of the whole East". Hürrem's influence opened the period known as the Sultanate of Women.

His image as an ideal ruler was shaped in his lifetime by commissioned works, above all those of Celalzade Mustafa, chancellor from 1534 to 1557. Later Ottoman writers of advice literature held up that image, urged sultans to keep the empire's institutions in their sixteenth-century form, and portrayed deviation from it as decline. Western historians long took such claims at face value and held that the empire declined after his death. Since the 1980s that view has been re-examined, and modern scholars overwhelmingly reject it; the following decades are described as an era of crisis, adaptation and transformation.

His names have their own history. "The Magnificent" is the Western epithet; Kanuni, "the Lawgiver", is absent from Ottoman sources of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and may date from the early eighteenth. The mausoleum raised at Turbék, near Szigetvár, where his heart and other organs were buried, became a place of pilgrimage. His is one of the 23 relief portraits of figures noted for their part in the principles of American law over the gallery doors of the House Chamber of the United States Capitol.

summary: Suleiman I ruled the Ottoman Empire from 1520 to 1566, the longest reign of any sultan. He took Belgrade, Rhodes, much of Hungary and Iraq, failed before Vienna, codified sultanic law and built the Süleymaniye. He had two of his sons put to death, and historians no longer hold that the empire declined after him.
references: Roger Bigelow Merriman, Suleiman the Magnificent, 1520–1566 (Harvard University Press, 1944)
Esin Atıl, The Age of Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (National Gallery of Art, 1987)
Caroline Finkel, Osman's Dream: The Story of the Ottoman Empire, 1300–1923 (Basic Books, 2005)
Gülru Necipoğlu, The Age of Sinan: Architectural Culture in the Ottoman Empire (Princeton University Press, 2005)
notes: Birth: 'probably on 6 November 1494, although this date is not known with absolute certainty', so circa is true.
Age at death: the article says 'at the age of 72' (Military campaigns) and 'at the age of 71' (Death and legacy); born 6 November 1494 and died 6 September 1566 makes 71. I gave no age.
'46 years' in the first takeaway is my subtraction (1520-1566); the article says only 'the longest reign among the Ottoman sultans'. Cut if arithmetic is not wanted.

Kanuni: the article contradicts itself. 'Alternative names' says the epithet is absent from 16th and 17th-century Ottoman sources and may date from the early 18th century; 'Legal and political reforms' says he 'was always Kanuni Suleiman ... to his Ottoman subjects'. 'deeds' follows the second, 'legacy' reports the first. The editor may wish to reword 'To his Ottoman subjects he was Kanuni' in deeds.

Ibrahim Pasha's execution: the article gives no year (only 'thirteen years as Grand Vizier' after 1523), so none is stated. Its remarks that Ibrahim was a 'possible lover' and that they 'slept together in the same bed' are left out.

Belgrade: '250,000 Turkish soldiers and over 100 ships' is the article's figure; it looks high but is copied. The article does not actually state the date Belgrade fell, only the encirclement on 28 August 1521 and (lead) 'Belgrade fell to him in 1521'.

Mustafa's death: the Succession section says 'the following summer' after 1552 in the Ereğli valley; the Sons list says executed 6 October 1553 at Konya. I gave the Ereğli valley and the date, not Konya.

Franco-Ottoman alliance: the article says Suleiman accepted Francis I's proposals after Tunis (1535) and the war with Venice 'the following year', and that Francis sought to renew it in 1542; no year is given for the first agreement, so I gave none.
The 1553/1554 firman: suggested by his doctor Moses Hamon; left the doctor out for space.
Left out: Indian Ocean details (Aceh 1564, Adal, Mughal correspondence), the tulip, the four-tiered crown of 1532, the Bender inscription, Shakespeare.

Wanted but not in the article: the year and place of Ibrahim's execution; the cause of Suleiman's death; the date Belgrade and Rhodes fell; the size of the Ottoman army at Mohács and Vienna; Selim I's deposition of Bayezid II and how Suleiman came to be the sole heir.
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js, or its Further reading list), chosen by the editor.
